name: PRP for stretch marks
lead: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) for stretch marks involves processing a person's own blood to concentrate platelets and then applying or injecting the product into stretch marks (striae distensae), often together with microneedling or fractional lasers. The aim is to make the marked skin look smoother and more even, and proponents say the growth factors released by platelets encourage collagen and elastin remodelling in the dermis.[7][8]

Stretch marks form when the dermis is stretched, for example during growth, weight change, muscle gain or pregnancy, and Wikipedia notes that a 2014 systematic review found no single treatment to be clearly effective once they have formed.[6] PRP is one of several procedures, alongside tretinoin, microneedling, lasers and carboxytherapy, that dermatology studies have compared.[14]

Published research consists of small comparative studies and registered trials, several of which combine PRP with another modality such as fractional lasers or fat grafting, which makes the contribution of PRP alone harder to separate. A 2021 systematic review included six studies and concluded that the supporting evidence was limited; a 2018 split-body study of 30 patients found improvement with both PRP and tretinoin, with PRP rated higher.[12][13]

Recent studies include a 2025 randomised split-abdomen comparison of microneedling with platelet-rich fibrin versus microneedling with PRP in 30 patients, in which both sides improved significantly without a statistically significant difference between them on the measured scores, and a 2026 review that described combination therapies including PRP as appearing superior to monotherapy, especially for older, paler stretch marks.[16]

angle.text: People use PRP as an add-on to microneedling or laser sessions, hoping to improve the texture and visibility of stretch marks on the abdomen, thighs, hips, shoulders or chest. Small split-body and comparative studies report clinical improvement in treated areas.

paras: PRP is made by drawing a patient's blood and centrifuging it to separate a platelet-rich fraction from red blood cells. Wikipedia describes the aim as concentrating platelets to roughly three to five times physiological levels, and notes that the product varies by person and by clinic kit.[7] A review of PRP's history and biology describes platelets as releasing growth factors that act on repair and remodelling processes.[8]

PRP for striae is described being used alone, with microneedling, after fractional laser, or with trichloroacetic acid peels.[14] PRP is also studied for other cosmetic skin concerns, such as a 2025 split-face trial comparing it with adipose stem-cell exosomes for photoaged facial skin.[10] Related products include platelet-rich fibrin (PRF), which a registered trial compares directly with PRP,[1] and nanofat or microfat grafting, which several registered trials combine with PRP.[3][4]

A 2021 systematic review in the International Wound Journal searched PubMed and Web of Science (June 2019) following PRISMA guidelines, found 12 studies and included 6; two had no control group and two used intra-individual comparisons, and all but one included histopathology. The authors concluded that the supporting evidence was limited.[11]

A 2018 study in Dermatologic Surgery treated 30 patients (27 women, 3 men) with bilateral striae, using intralesional PRP on one side and topical 0.05 percent tretinoin on the other. Both sides improved significantly, PRP was rated more effective for clinical improvement (p = .015) and patient satisfaction (p = .003), and biopsies after treatment showed increased collagen and elastic fibres in all patients.[12][13]

Other published comparisons listed in PubMed include PRP versus carboxytherapy and tripolar radiofrequency (2019), fractional CO2 laser with and without PRP (2023), and microneedling alone versus microneedling with PRP for stretch marks and post-surgical scars (2024).[14]

Wikipedia reports low adverse-effect rates for PRP in most trials, since the material comes from the patient's own blood.[7] It also reports a 2024 CDC account of three women diagnosed with HIV after "vampire facials" at an unlicensed New Mexico spa that reused equipment without sterilisation, which has been cited in discussion of PRP-microneedling hygiene.[7] Injection and microneedling can cause pain, redness, bruising and swelling in the treated area.

Wikipedia traces the term "platelet-rich plasma" to 1954 and an early surgical use to open-heart surgery in Italy in 1987; PRP was considered for hair loss from about 2006, and microneedling with PRP, popularised in the 2010s as the "vampire facial", is now a common aesthetic service.[7] Wikipedia states that the FDA does not regulate PRP itself but clears the devices used to prepare it, so uses such as stretch-mark treatment are off-label.[7] Stretch-mark studies come mainly from dermatology departments and are reported in dermatology journals.[9][14]

Stretch marks (striae distensae) form when rapid growth or stretching tears the dermis, as in puberty, pregnancy, weight gain or muscle gain; higher cortisol and corticosteroid use can make them more likely by reducing skin pliability and collagen and elastin production.[6] Reference summaries estimate that a large share of pregnant women, often quoted at 50 to 90 percent, develop striae, with risk rising with younger age, higher BMI and greater weight gain.[6]

Early marks are reddish or purple (striae rubra) and over time they atrophy, lose pigment and become paler, softer and slightly depressed (striae alba).[6] They pose no inherent health risk but can cause distress, which is why people look for ways to reduce their visibility, including lifters and people who have lost weight rapidly.[6] Summaries state that there is no clearly effective treatment once marks form, and that a Cochrane review found no evidence that creams or oils prevent or reduce stretch marks in pregnancy; tretinoin has shown benefit on early marks in several studies but is a known animal teratogen.[6]

PRP is prepared from a person's own blood and concentrates platelets, which release growth factors that are thought to stimulate fibroblasts and collagen production.[7][8] The idea for striae is that the stored growth factors could help rebuild the thinned dermis. PRP is usually delivered in dermatology by injection or applied to the skin after microneedling or fractional laser so that it can pass into the dermis through the created channels.[9]

This rationale also explains why PRP is rarely used alone for stretch marks in the research record. Registered trials compare or combine it with fractional CO2 laser, microneedling, nanofat grafting or fibrin-based preparations (PRF), so improvements are usually attributed to the combined protocol.[1][3][4][5]

Registered and published studies place PRP alongside tretinoin cream, carboxytherapy, nanofat and microfat grafting, fractional laser, PRF, and even exosome preparations from adipose-derived stem cells, reflecting a field still working out which approach, if any, gives the most consistent change in striae colour and texture.[1][2][3][4][10][13] Findings summarised in the systematic review of PRP for striae are covered under Clinical studies.

Microneedling, also called collagen induction therapy or dermarolling, repeatedly punctures the skin with fine sterile needles and is used for scarring and acne. PRP from the patient's own blood can be applied during or after treatment or injected into scars; the combination is sometimes marketed as a 'vampire facial'. Wikipedia states that the added benefit of PRP is still unproven pending further studies.[18]

The main safety concern raised is infection when such procedures are performed outside medical settings without infection-control training. In April 2024 the CDC reported three HIV diagnoses among clients of an Albuquerque spa that offered vampire facials, while nearly 200 other former clients and partners tested negative, as summarised by Wikipedia.[18][7]

A 2025 randomised comparative study in Archives of Dermatological Research treated 30 patients (27 women, 3 men) with abdominal stretch marks using microneedling with PRF on one side and microneedling with PRP on the other, three monthly sessions. Both methods improved striae significantly; the PRF side performed better numerically, but differences in Davey score, stripe width, global assessment and patient satisfaction were not statistically significant.[16]

A 2026 exploratory study in Tissue & Cell followed six women with post-pregnancy atrophic abdominal striae, three treated with saline and three with PRP weekly for 12 weeks. PRP was associated with thickened collagen bundles, better fibre organisation and a denser elastic fibre network on tissue analysis; the authors state the small sample precludes causal conclusions.[16]

A 2026 review of stretch-mark treatments reported modest efficacy for tretinoin, collagen remodelling with lasers, and combination therapies including PRP appearing superior to monotherapy, especially for striae alba, while noting heterogeneous studies and inconsistent outcome measures.[16] A 2026 scoping review of PRP for immature post-traumatic scars and early keloids covered five studies with 65 patients and described the evidence as extremely limited, with no serious adverse events reported; it concerns scars rather than striae.[16]

Wikipedia describes PRP as marketed for wrinkles, fine lines and hair loss, with a 2024 meta-analysis reporting positive effects on venous and diabetic foot ulcers, tentative support in knee osteoarthritis, and mixed or weak evidence for several tendon conditions. The World Anti-Doping Agency removed intramuscular PRP from its prohibited list in January 2011.[7] Because lifters often look for tendon and joint care, many community PRP discussions concern those uses rather than skin.[15]

sections.h: Stretch marks in lifters and growing bodies
paras: Stretch marks are associated with skin stretching and dermal tearing during rapid growth such as puberty or pregnancy, with weight gain and corticosteroid exposure also named as contributors; teenagers appear at highest risk of severe striae, according to Wikipedia.[17] Wikipedia describes no clearly useful treatments and reports that tretinoin appeared effective on early marks in several studies while a systematic review found no evidence creams or oils prevent or reduce stretch marks in pregnancy.[17] A 2026 case report described a 15-year-old with extensive striae after prolonged topical clobetasol use, illustrating the corticosteroid link.[16]

NCT07561671, a 30-person trial started in February 2024 and listed as completed, compares PRP with PRF in striae distensae.[1] NCT07001644, a 50-person trial begun in 2022 with unknown status, compares microneedling with carboxytherapy in red stretch marks and appears in PRP-related searches rather than testing PRP itself.[2]

Three small registered studies test combinations: nanofat grafting plus PRP versus microfat grafting plus PRP (12 participants, 2019);[3] fractional laser plus PRP versus nanofat grafting plus PRP in striae gravidarum (10 participants, phase 3, 2017);[4] and fractional carbon dioxide laser combined with PRP in striae gravidarum (16 participants, phase 3, completed).[5] The registry records do not list outcomes. Published comparative studies are summarised under Effectiveness.[12][13]
Additional studies since 2025 are described under Recent studies, including a 30-patient randomised comparison of PRP and PRF with microneedling and an exploratory six-woman histology study.[16]

PRP appears in skin and body-improvement discussions as an add-on to microneedling or laser treatment for scars, texture and stretch marks. Forum threads captured for this topic mostly concern PRP for tendons, joints and hair rather than striae, so community claims specific to stretch marks are sparse.[15]

card.summary: Concentrated platelets from your own blood, tried on stretch marks mostly as an add-on in small trials.
card.note: Registered studies are small and mostly combine PRP with other treatments; no results were reviewed.

quick.overview:
PRP is made from a person's own blood and has been tried on stretch marks, usually together with microneedling, lasers or fat grafting.
Its effect on stretch marks is not established; the evidence is a handful of small registered trials with no listed results.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say platelet growth factors stimulate collagen and tissue repair in the skin.
quick.risks: As a blood-derived injectable procedure, it is performed by clinicians.
